comment: Every command shown on the website. scripts/check-website-examples.py runs them in this order, in one directory, against OpenSSL 3.5 and 4.1 (CI job `website-examples`). A task with status `supported` is also run with baldssl in place of openssl and must produce the same output and files. `deterministic: false` marks commands whose output is random (keys, serials), compared on exit status only. Sections: `tasks` (Common tasks), `install`, `usage`, `compatibility`.

examples.title: Create a private key
examples.explanation: Generates an elliptic-curve private key on the P-256 curve and writes it to key.pem in PKCS#8 PEM format. The file is a secret: anyone holding it can act as you.

examples.title: Create an Ed25519 private key
examples.explanation: Ed25519 keys are small and fast, and are used for SSH, signatures and recent TLS deployments.

examples.title: Create an RSA private key
examples.explanation: RSA is still the most widely deployed key type. 3072 bits is the size NIST SP 800-57 associates with 128-bit security.

examples.title: Inspect a private key
examples.explanation: Prints the key's type, size and components. Useful to check what a key file actually contains.

examples.title: Extract the public key
examples.explanation: Writes the public half of the key, which is safe to share, to pub.pem.

examples.title: Create a certificate signing request (CSR)
examples.explanation: A CSR carries your public key and the name you want certified. You send it to a certificate authority (CA), which returns a signed certificate.

examples.title: Inspect a CSR
examples.explanation: Shows what a CSR asks for before you submit it.

examples.title: Create a self-signed CA certificate
examples.explanation: Creates a new key (ca-key.pem) and a certificate for it, signed by itself, valid for 10 years. This is the root of a private certificate authority.
examples.command: openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -noenc -keyout ca-key.pem -out ca.crt -days 3650 -subj "/CN=Example CA"

examples.title: Sign a CSR with your CA
examples.explanation: Issues a certificate valid for 90 days for the request, signed by the CA. -CAcreateserial keeps the serial numbers in ca.srl.
examples.command: openssl x509 -req -in request.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca-key.pem -CAcreateserial -days 90 -out cert.crt

examples.title: Read a certificate
examples.explanation: Prints every field of a certificate: who it is for, who issued it, when it expires, its public key and its extensions.

examples.title: Show who a certificate is for and who issued it
examples.explanation: The subject is the certificate's owner, the issuer is the CA that signed it.

examples.title: Check when a certificate expires
examples.explanation: Prints the start and end of the validity period. Expired certificates are a common cause of outages.

examples.title: Compute a certificate's fingerprint
examples.explanation: The SHA-256 hash of the certificate, used to compare or pin certificates.

examples.title: Convert a certificate from PEM to DER
examples.explanation: PEM is the text form (BEGIN CERTIFICATE ...), DER the binary form some systems (Java, Windows) expect.

examples.title: Convert a certificate from DER to PEM
examples.explanation: The reverse conversion, back to the text form.

examples.title: Verify a certificate against a CA
examples.explanation: Checks the signature and the validity period, and prints cert.crt: OK when the chain is valid.

examples.title: Check that a key matches a certificate
examples.explanation: A certificate and a key belong together when their public keys are equal. Writes both public keys and prints match when they are identical; any failing step stops the command.
examples.command: openssl x509 -in cert.crt -noout -pubkey > cert-pub.pem && openssl pkey -in key.pem -pubout > key-pub.pem && cmp cert-pub.pem key-pub.pem && echo match

examples.title: Bundle a key and its certificates into PKCS#12
examples.explanation: A .p12 (or .pfx) file holds a key and its certificate chain, protected by a password. Browsers, Windows and Java import this format.
examples.command: openssl pkcs12 -export -inkey key.pem -in cert.crt -certfile ca.crt -out bundle.p12 -passout pass:changeit

examples.title: Extract a PKCS#12 bundle
examples.explanation: Writes the key and certificates of a .p12 file to a PEM file, without encrypting the key.

examples.title: See the certificate a server presents
examples.explanation: Connects to a TLS server and prints who its certificate is for, who issued it and when it expires.
examples.command: openssl s_client -connect github.com:443 -servername github.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates

examples.title: Hash a file
examples.explanation: Prints the SHA-256 digest of a file, to check that a download is intact.

examples.title: Generate random bytes
examples.explanation: Prints 32 random bytes in hexadecimal, for example as a secret token.

examples.title: Encrypt a file with a password
examples.explanation: Encrypts with AES-256 and derives the key from the password with PBKDF2.

examples.title: Decrypt a file
examples.explanation: Decrypts the file encrypted above, with the same password and options.

examples.title: Encode a file in base64
examples.explanation: Turns binary data into text that can be pasted into an email or a configuration file.

examples.title: Hash a password for /etc/shadow
examples.explanation: Produces a SHA-512 crypt hash, the format Linux uses for login passwords.
examples.command: openssl passwd -6 -salt examplesalt 'correct horse battery staple'

examples.title: Show the OpenSSL version
examples.explanation: Prints the installed version, the first thing to check when a command behaves differently between machines.
